$comment: Handwritten faces shared by every approach. They are accents that sit on top of a product's pairing; they never replace it. A product picks at most one in products/<product>/brand.json -> typography.hand, and only from the faces its style allows (approaches/<id>/typography.json -> handwritten). All are free Google Fonts (SIL Open Font License or Apache 2.0, as noted). Designer, licence, weights and scripts come from each family's METADATA.pb in the google/fonts repository. The evidence behind the rules is in foundations/research/handwriting.json.

tiers.$comment: How much reading a face can carry. Hand faces are less familiar than book faces, so they cost more effort per word (see the fluency and credibility findings). Size factors are rules of thumb: hand faces have smaller, irregular x-heights, so they need more size to look as big as the body text.

read.label: Readable
read.summary: Unjoined, even print. Can carry a short sentence: a note, a sticker, a subhead.
roles: headline (only in styles that allow hand headlines)

glance.label: Glance
glance.summary: Quick pen or marker. A few words that are read in one look.
roles: price tag (word only, not the number)

display.label: Display only
display.summary: Connected scripts and scrawls. One to three words, large.
display.minSize: Headline size (at least 3 x body); never under 24 px on screen

fonts.designer: Shantell Martin, Arrow Type, Anya Danilova
fonts.mood: The artist Shantell Martin's marker hand, drawn as a full type family. Monoline and unjoined; the informality axis makes letters wobble so repeats look less like a font.
fonts.useFor: Notes, stickers and friendly subheads; the only face here that can carry a short paragraph in a pinch.
fonts.avoidFor: Anything that must look official or exact.
fonts.sample: Made this morning, just for you

fonts.mood: Neat, unjoined print with even spacing, like a careful teacher's board writing. Calm, not childish.
fonts.useFor: Annotations next to illustrations, menu notes, short tips.
fonts.avoidFor: Headlines that need weight: it has one regular weight.
fonts.sample: Ask us what came out of the oven

fonts.mood: Pen handwriting designed for Devanagari and Latin together, so bilingual notes match in size and rhythm.
fonts.useFor: Hindi and English notes, shopkeeper boards, labels for Indian audiences.
fonts.avoidFor: Long Devanagari text: its letters are informal and slightly slanted.

fonts.mood: Soft, round, childlike pencil print with a Korean companion. The roundest hand here.
fonts.useFor: Sweet food, kids, gentle care, Korean and English notes.
fonts.avoidFor: Serious or premium products: it reads young.

fonts.mood: Squared, upright draughtsman's print, like notes on a plan or a sketchbook diagram.
fonts.useFor: Labels on sketches and diagrams, measurements in words, how-it's-made notes.
fonts.avoidFor: Warm or emotional lines: it reads technical.

fonts.mood: A quick ballpoint note, narrow and fluent. Fits margins and small spaces.
fonts.useFor: Margin notes, arrows with a word, 'from us' sign-offs, scrapbook notes.
fonts.avoidFor: Small sizes: its x-height is low, so it shrinks faster than it looks.

fonts.mood: Caveat drawn with a brush pen: thicker, wetter, a little louder.
fonts.useFor: Short labels on colour, sign-painting notes, mid-century accents.
fonts.avoidFor: Next to Caveat itself: use one or the other.

fonts.mood: Bold, round felt-tip print with a bouncy baseline. Playful and loud enough for doodle headlines.
fonts.useFor: Doodle headlines and labels, kids, games, playful launches.

fonts.mood: Chunky felt marker, mostly capitals. Written on a box, a tape strip or a sign in a hurry.
fonts.useFor: Labels on kraft paper or tape, stickers, tags, one word on a poster.
fonts.avoidFor: More than a few words: it is all-capitals in feel and tiring to read.

fonts.mood: A thin, fast pen, like a diary or a note on a photo. Very light; needs size and contrast.
fonts.useFor: Captions on photos in a scrapbook, diary notes, Korean and English notes.
fonts.avoidFor: Busy or mid-tone grounds: its strokes are thin.

fonts.mood: Fast dry-brush marker with movement and texture in the strokes.
fonts.useFor: Street, music and surf accents, tags on photos, one energetic word.

fonts.designer: Vernon Adams, Jacques Le Bailly, Botjo Nikoltchev, Ani Petrova
fonts.mood: Heavy, connected 1950s American surf script. Very familiar, so it reads fast, but it is widely used: pair it with something unexpected.
fonts.useFor: One word or a logotype-style sign-off on surf, summer and retro pieces.
fonts.avoidFor: Anything that should feel original on its own; more than three words.

fonts.mood: Slanted connected brush script in the spirit of 1930s-50s sign-painting and advertising.
fonts.useFor: A single word or sign-off in mid-century pieces: 'Fresh', 'Since 1952', a product name in a swash.
fonts.avoidFor: All capitals (connected scripts break apart), small sizes.

fonts.mood: Lively connected script with a bouncing baseline. Warmer and lighter than Yellowtail.
fonts.useFor: Invitations, a thank-you line, a personal sign-off.
fonts.avoidFor: Anything functional; small sizes; all capitals.

fonts.mood: Energetic brush script with dry edges, like a quick sign or a sports badge.
fonts.useFor: One energetic word on surf, sport or street pieces.
fonts.avoidFor: Calm pieces; anything longer than three words.

fonts.mood: A loose pencil scrawl, like a note to yourself. The least readable face here, which is the point.
fonts.useFor: A scribbled aside in a scrapbook ('this one!'), one or two words.
fonts.avoidFor: Anything a reader needs; small sizes.

fonts.mood: Rough, wide marker capitals with a skate-and-punk edge.
fonts.useFor: One shouted word on a neon-surf or gig poster.
fonts.avoidFor: Anything longer than three words; quiet products.

rules: Hand faces are accents. One per piece, added to the product's pairing; never the body text.
Keep inside the face's tier: readable up to 12 words, glance up to 6, display up to 3.

Never for body copy, legal text, prices or numbers people compare, data and charts, step-by-step instructions, or the call-to-action button. Hard-to-read type makes the task itself seem harder, and hand-drawn type lowers trust in data.
Size up: at least the tier's minimum size, and contrast of 4.5:1 or more against the ground (hand strokes are thin and irregular).
Sentence case. Never set a connected script in capitals, never letter-space it, never fake bold, italic or outline it.

Fit the product: hand type helps warm, caring, indulgent, gift, food and health-focused products and new or small brands. It adds little for brands people already love, and it hurts functional, technical, risky, financial and data-led messages.
Use a face that covers the language: Kalam for Devanagari, Gaegu or Nanum Pen Script for Korean. Never let a missing script fall back to a system font.
Real lettering drawn for the piece beats any font. When using a font, avoid repeated identical words side by side, which give it away; Shantell Sans's informality axis helps.
Only where the product's style allows it (approaches/<id>/typography.json -> handwritten), and only the faces it lists.
